scenes.text: Walking through a doorway can really make you forget why you went into the room.
Scientists call it the doorway effect, or the location updating effect.
Psychologist Gabriel Radvansky at the University of Notre Dame tested this in two thousand eleven.
In a video game, people picked up objects and carried them from table to table.
Sometimes the next table was in another room, and sometimes in the same room, the same distance away.
Along the way, their memory of the objects was tested.
People forgot more often right after passing through a doorway.
Then the team tried it in real rooms, with real boxes, and found the same thing.
Going back to the room where they started didn't help them remember.
Scientists think your brain treats a doorway as an event boundary, like the end of a chapter.
It files away the old scene and starts a new one.
That saves effort, but your reason for walking in can get stuck in the old file.
Later studies found the effect shows up most when your mind is juggling lots of things at once.
So when you forget why you came in, the doorway might really be partly to blame.
Has a doorway ever wiped your mind clean?

title: Why doorways make you forget things 🚪
caption: The 'doorway effect': in Notre Dame experiments, people forgot more right after walking through a doorway. Scientists think the brain treats doorways as event boundaries. 🧠
